method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **Usually self-limiting, resolving without complications**; management centres on hydration and analgesia.
claims.source_text: HSV gingivostomatitis is usually a self-limiting illness, which resolves without complications … Management is focused on ensuring adequate hydration and analgesia
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Typical age 6 months–5 years**, though older children and adolescents are affected too. **Neonatal HSV is severe and not covered here.**
claims.source_text: Typical age is 6 months – 5 years, although can occur in older children and adolescents … Neonatal HSV can be severe with significant morbidity and mortality; it is not covered in this guideline
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Onset is about one week after contact with a shedder**, after a prodrome of fever, anorexia, malaise and headache. **Lesions heal in about 10–14 days (up to 3 weeks if severe).**
claims.source_text: Primary HSV infection occurs approximately one week after contact with a person shedding HSV (who is often asymptomatic) … Usually begins with a prodrome which may include fever, anorexia, malaise and headache … Lesions heal in approximately 10-14 days (up to 3 weeks in severe cases)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Vesicles on the buccal mucosa, tongue, gums, hard palate, pharynx, lips and perioral skin**; yellow with a red halo once ruptured; they bleed easily and may crust black.
claims.source_text: Vesicles can be found on the buccal mucosa, tongue, gingiva, hard palate, pharynx, lips and perioral skin … Lesions appear yellow after the vesicles rupture and develop a red halo. Vesicles bleed easily and can develop a black crust
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Differentials:** hand, foot and mouth disease · herpangina · aphthous ulcers · Stevens-Johnson syndrome · Behçet syndrome · RIME.
claims.source_text: Differential diagnoses Hand foot and mouth disease Herpangina Aphthous ulcers Stevens-Johnson Syndrome Behcet syndrome Reactive infectious mucocutaneous eruption (RIME)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Lethargy, drowsiness, focal neurology or altered behaviour: think HSV encephalitis.**
claims.source_text: Lethargy, drowsiness or focal neurology and altered behaviour should raise concern for HSV encephalitis
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Dehydration is the most common complication and the usual reason for admission.** Painful vesicles can cause refusal to drink.
claims.source_text: Hospitalisation is most often required due to dehydration … Assess hydration as dehydration is the most common complication … Oral vesicles may be very painful, resulting in refusal to drink
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Other complications:** herpetic whitlow (thumb-suckers), herpetic keratitis, oesophagitis, pneumonitis, lip adhesions, secondary infection. **Examine the eyes and nervous system.**
claims.source_text: Complications include herpetic whitlow (often in children who suck their thumb), herpetic keratitis, oesophagitis, pneumonitis, lip adhesions and secondary infections … Examine for complications (neurological and eye examination)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider secondary infection if the child worsens (e.g. new fever) after a period of gradual recovery.**
claims.source_text: Secondary infections are uncommon but should be considered if there is worsening of the child's symptoms (eg new onset of fever) after a period of gradual recovery
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Diagnosis is clinical.** Where confirmation is needed (immunocompromised host or contact), send a flocked lesion swab for PCR; **serology is rarely helpful.**
claims.source_text: Diagnosis is clinical and, in most cases, does not require laboratory confirmation … Where confirmation is required (immunocompromised host or contact), swab lesion (flocked swab) for PCR … Serology is rarely helpful
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Offer analgesia to all: paracetamol and ibuprofen.** Severe pain may need admission and oral opioids.
claims.source_text: Consider in all children with oral HSV … Simple oral analgesia including paracetamol and ibuprofen … For severe pain, inpatient management and oral opiates may be required
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Topical anaesthetics are commonly used but unproven** (e.g. Xylocaine Viscous, lignocaine gel 2%, Mucosoothe); under 3 years, apply with a cotton swab.
claims.source_text: While not shown to be efficacious, topical analgesics are commonly used eg Xylocaine Viscous®, Lignocaine gel 2%®, Mucosoothe® (in children <3 years, apply to affected areas with a cotton swab)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Mild or no dehydration: most can go home without a fluid trial**, with advice and scheduled review.
claims.source_text: Most children with mild or no dehydration can be discharged without a trial of fluids, after appropriate advice and scheduled review
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Moderate dehydration: consider an ORS trial of 10–20 mL/kg over 1 hour**, in small frequent volumes after analgesia. Severe dehydration or failed rehydration may need NG or IV fluids.
claims.source_text: For moderate dehydration, a trial of oral rehydration solution (ORS) 10-20 mL/kg over 1 hour can be considered - give small frequent volumes after analgesia … Severe dehydration or failure of rehydration may necessitate NGT or IV rehydration
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Immunocompromised: aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV 8-hourly until no new lesions.**
claims.source_text: Treat immunocompromised children with aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV 8 hourly until there are no new lesions
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Immunocompetent children generally need no antiviral.** Within 72 hours of onset, with severe pain or dehydration, **consider aciclovir 10 mg/kg (max 400 mg) orally 5 times a day until no new lesions.**
claims.source_text: Immunocompetent children generally do not require antiviral treatment. However, if within 72 hr of onset of disease and in cases of severe pain or dehydration, consider aciclovir 10 mg/kg (max 400 mg) oral 5 times per day until there are no new lesions
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Topical aciclovir is not effective.**
claims.source_text: Topical aciclovir is not effective
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Exclude from childcare or school until the sores have dried** if the child cannot control oral secretions. Barrier cream on the lips can prevent adhesions.
claims.source_text: Children with gingivostomatitis, who do not have control of oral secretions, should be excluded from childcare/school until sores have dried … Barrier cream (eg petroleum jelly) to the lips can prevent adhesions
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Involve the paediatric team for:** inadequate hydration · immunocompromise · severe pain, keratitis, pneumonitis, eczema herpeticum or encephalitis · a need for IV aciclovir.
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with local paediatric team when Unable to maintain adequate hydration Immunocompromised Severe pain, keratitis, pneumonitis, eczema herpeticum, encephalitis IV aciclovir required
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discharge when drinking enough to stay hydrated**, or when follow-up is arranged.
claims.source_text: Consider discharge when The child is drinking adequate volumes to maintain hydration or follow up is arranged
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'HSV Gingivostomatitis' (Last updated November 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/HSV_Gingivostomatitis/, retrieved 2026-09-23
